analysis.evidence: Pharaoh is the caller, and לְאַבְרָם identifies Abram as the person he summons. The following וַיֹּאמֶר introduces Pharaoh’s questions to Abram.
analysis.morphology: The prefixed conjunction וַ marks the narrative sequence. The verb is Qal wayyiqtol, third-person masculine singular, with Pharaoh as its subject.

evidence.note: Pharaoh calls Abram and asks why he concealed that Sarai was his wife.
The words מֶלֶךְ מִצְרָיִם, “king of Egypt,” identify Pharaoh’s office.

article.name: פַּרְעֹה
article.summary: Pharaoh is the title of Egypt’s king. In Genesis 12 the ruler bearing this title summons Abram and questions him about Sarai.

draft.change: Add a name article for the Egyptian royal title. The source gloss “lye; potash” does not fit the speaker, and the proposed Hebrew root פרע has no support here.
draft.definition: Pharaoh, the royal title borne by the king of Egypt.
draft.evidence: Genesis 12:18 identifies Pharaoh as the speaker who summons Abram. Exodus 6:11 explicitly calls the ruler פַּרְעֹה מֶלֶךְ מִצְרָיִם, “Pharaoh king of Egypt.”

analysis.evidence: In וַיִּקְרָא פַרְעֹה לְאַבְרָם, Pharaoh is the subject of “called” and לְאַבְרָם identifies the person he summons. Pharaoh then addresses Abram directly, asking why Abram failed to tell him that Sarai was his wife.
analysis.morphology: Hebrew proper noun. The royal title stands alone, with no prefix or suffix, and takes masculine singular agreement in וַיִּקְרָא and וַיֹּאמֶר.
analysis.sense: The title of the king of Egypt, used here of the ruler who summons Abram.

draft.change: Link the existing Abram article to אבה through its father element and add Genesis 12:4 as an example.
draft.definition: Abram, son of Terah, later named Abraham. The name means “exalted father.”
draft.evidence: Genesis 12:4 repeats the name אַבְרָם when giving Abram’s age at departure. The name’s אָב element belongs to Haqor’s אבה article.

analysis.evidence: וַיִּקְרָא פַרְעֹה לְאַבְרָם means “Pharaoh called for Abram.” Pharaoh then addresses Abram directly, asking why he did not say that she was his wife.
analysis.morphology: The preposition לְ marks Abram, a personal name, as the person Pharaoh calls.
analysis.sense: Abram, the son of Terah later named Abraham

analysis.morphology: Qal wayyiqtol, third person masculine singular, with prefixed וַ־

analysis.evidence: Pharaoh asks Abram מַה זֹּאת עָשִׂיתָ לִּי, “What is this you have done to me?” מַה asks what Abram has done. The following question uses לָמָּה to ask why he did not tell Pharaoh.
analysis.morphology: Uninflected interrogative pronoun with no prefix or suffix.

analysis.evidence: Carried forward: this word and its source tagging were reviewed identically at 66570:2, 66318:6.
analysis.morphology: Qal perfect, second person masculine singular. The ending ־תָ marks the subject.

draft.change: Add Genesis 12:18 as an example of the existing Hebrew sense why-for-what-purpose.
draft.definition: With prefixed לְ, מָה asks for a reason.
draft.evidence: Genesis 12:18 uses לָמָּה to ask why Abram withheld the fact that Sarai was his wife.

analysis.evidence: In לָמָּה לֹא הִגַּדְתָּ לִּי כִּי אִשְׁתְּךָ הִוא, Pharaoh asks Abram why he did not tell him that she was his wife. The question concerns the reason for Abram’s silence.
analysis.morphology: The prefixed preposition לְ appears as לָ before the interrogative מָה, with doubling of מ. Together they form the question word לָמָּה, ‘why?’
analysis.sense: With לְ, asks the reason for an action or omission.

analysis.evidence: In לָמָּה לֹא הִגַּדְתָּ לִּי, “Why did you not tell me?”, לֹא negates הִגַּדְתָּ, “you told.” Pharaoh asks why Abram failed to tell him that she was Abram’s wife.
analysis.morphology: Hebrew negative particle with no prefix or suffix.

analysis.evidence: Pharaoh asks Abram, “Why didn’t you tell me that she was your wife?” לִּי identifies Pharaoh as the recipient, and כִּי אִשְׁתְּךָ הִוא gives the fact Abram failed to report.
analysis.morphology: Hiphil perfect, second person masculine singular. The ending ־תָּ marks Abram as the person addressed.
analysis.sense: tell someone that something is the case

analysis.evidence: In לָמָּה לֹא הִגַּדְתָּ לִּי כִּי אִשְׁתְּךָ הִוא, “Why did you not tell me that she is your wife?”, כִּי introduces the statement Pharaoh expected Abram to tell him.
analysis.morphology: Hebrew conjunction with no prefix or suffix.
analysis.sense: that (what is seen, known or said)

analysis.evidence: Pharaoh asks Abram why he did not tell him כִּי אִשְׁתְּךָ הִוא, “that she is your wife.” The suffix identifies Abram as her husband.
analysis.morphology: The feminine singular common noun is in the construct state with the second-person masculine singular possessive suffix ךָ, referring to Abram.

analysis.evidence: In כִּי אִשְׁתְּךָ הִוא, “that she is your wife,” הִוא refers to Sarai and serves as the subject. אִשְׁתְּךָ, “your wife,” is the predicate.
analysis.morphology: Independent third-person feminine singular pronoun, written הִוא and read הִיא.
